screens.title: CIA Triad: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
screens.narratorSegment: The CIA triad is a compact way to reason about what security must achieve. Confidentiality means only authorized parties can read sensitive information. A practical example is encrypting customer records at rest and encrypting service-to-service traffic to prevent eavesdropping. A common misconception is that encryption alone resolves confidentiality; keys and access controls matter too. Integrity means data remains accurate and unmodified except by authorized actions. Use hashing, digital signatures, and strict write controls to detect or prevent tampering — for example, signing configuration blobs to ensure they weren't altered before deployment. A mistake here is relying solely on network transport protection and ignoring storage integrity checks. Availability ensures authorized users can access systems when needed. Techniques include redundancy, failover, backups, and rate limiting to defend against denial-of-service. Overemphasizing confidentiality or integrity while ignoring availability can make systems unusable, so tradeoffs matter. For instance, excessively strict authentication may block legitimate traffic during peak load. When designing a service, name which of the three goals are most critical for each component, then pick controls that align with those priorities. What would you prioritize for a payment processor versus a public catalog?

keyIdea.title: CIA Takeaway
keyIdea.text: Treat confidentiality, integrity, and availability as primary design constraints; pick controls that match each component's priority.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › CIA Triad
CIA triad — definitions
Confidentiality
Limit data access to authorized entities. Example: encrypt database at rest and TLS for service traffic.
Integrity
Ensure data correctness and authenticity. Example: use hashes and signatures to detect tampering.
Availability
Keep systems reachable for authorized users. Example: redundancy, backups, and DoS protections.
Common misconception
Mistaking one control, like encryption, as a complete solution. Controls must be paired with key management and access policies.
Why it matters
Balancing the triad helps prioritize work: a payment ledger values integrity and availability more than public catalog confidentiality.
Concrete scenario
Designing a checkout service: customer payment data requires high confidentiality and integrity, while product browsing requires high availability but lower secrecy requirements. For the checkout path, mandate encryption at rest and in transit, signed transaction logs, strict access controls, and redundancy for availability.
Key Takeaway

Explicitly declare which CIA goals each service must meet and choose controls that directly address them.

Check your understanding: Which single control helps both confidentiality and integrity for stored data? (Answer: encryption plus integrity checks like authenticated encryption or signatures.)

screens.title: Confidentiality in Practice
screens.narratorSegment: Confidentiality protects data from unauthorized disclosure. In practical systems, confidentiality is implemented with layered mechanisms: encryption of data at rest, transport encryption between services, and strict access controls that limit who can read sensitive fields. A concrete example is storing customer payment details: the database should use disk or column-level encryption, communication channels should use TLS, and application roles should deny direct read access except for tokenized or masked views. Key management is frequently the weak link—if encryption keys are stored alongside data, confidentiality is broken. Rotation, limited key access, and hardware security modules are typical mitigations. Another common pitfall is assuming transport-only protection suffices; someone with database access will still read unencrypted data. Practical checks include threat-modeling who can access the database servers and ensuring backups and logs are also encrypted. Finally, consider least privilege: both human and service accounts should have the minimal read rights necessary. A short takeaway: encryption plus proper key lifecycle and access control is the correct pattern, not encryption alone. How would you protect backups and logs that contain the same sensitive fields? Confidentiality in Practice means use layered confidentiality: encrypt data, protect keys, and apply least privilege to human and service access.. In practical terms, encryption, access control, and common pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Confidentiality
Core controls
  • • Encrypt data at rest using managed keys or hardware modules.
  • • Use TLS for data in transit between services.
  • • Apply least-privilege access controls for services and people.
  • • Protect backups and logs with the same encryption and access rules.
Pitfall
Storing keys next to encrypted data or relying only on transport security leaves sensitive information exposed at rest.
Concrete example
An e-commerce checkout stores card tokens in a database. Use column encryption, rotate keys periodically, restrict read access to the payment microservice, and ensure backups are encrypted. For logs, redact payment fields or send them to a separate, secured logging system.
Key Takeaway

Confidentiality requires encryption plus key controls and least privilege; treat backups and logs as equally sensitive.

Check your understanding
Who should be allowed to decrypt production payment data: operations engineers, customer support, or a dedicated payment service? (Answer: only the payment service with audited access.)

screens.title: Integrity — Detecting and Preventing Tampering
screens.narratorSegment: Integrity assures that data is complete, accurate, and authentic. Practically, this means detecting unauthorized changes and preventing them where possible. Common mechanisms include cryptographic hashes to detect modification, digital signatures to bind content to an identity, and tightly scoped write permissions so only authorized services can change a record. For example, sign configuration files so deployment agents can verify they are unchanged. Consider a misconfigured microservice that accepts client-supplied metadata and writes it directly to a shared database — a tampering risk. To mitigate, validate inputs, use role-based write permissions, and add end-to-end integrity checks such as message authentication codes when data moves between services. Another misconception is assuming transport-level integrity fixes storage tampering; it doesn't. Transport protections only ensure correctness in transit, not against a compromised storage subsystem. A closing question to consider: for your most critical data, would you add tamper-evident logs, signatures, or both, and why? Integrity — Detecting and Preventing Tampering means combine detection (hashes, signatures) with prevention (access controls, input validation) to protect data correctness.. In practical terms, hashes, signatures, and strict write controls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Integrity
Mechanisms for integrity
  • • Hashes and message authentication codes detect unexpected changes.
  • • Digital signatures tie data to an identity and enable non-repudiation.
  • • Access control and input validation prevent unauthorized writes.
  • • Tamper-evident logs help forensic and audit needs.
Misconception
Believing transport integrity solves storage integrity. Systems need end-to-end checks that include storage and backups.
Example
An audit trail signs each change to a financial ledger. Before accepting an entry, the system verifies the signature and the previous hash to ensure the chain is unbroken. If a signature fails, alerts trigger and writes are rejected until the source is reconciled.
Key Takeaway

Use both preventive controls and detection mechanisms to maintain integrity; detection alone is not enough for critical systems.

Check
Would you require signatures for configuration changes in production? If yes, how would you manage keys and verification?

screens.title: Availability: Designing for Resilience
screens.narratorSegment: Availability ensures authorized users can reach services when they need them. Designing for availability means planning for hardware failures, software bugs, and malicious traffic. Practical strategies include redundancy across instances and zones, automated failover, regular backups with tested recovery procedures, and capacity planning. To defend against denial-of-service attacks, employ rate limiting, load shedding, and Web Application Firewalls; for large-scale attacks, use network-level protections and upstream scrubbing services. A common mistake is treating availability as purely an operational concern; architects must design systems with availability goals in mind, for example by selecting stateless services where possible and separating critical services into independent failure domains. Another tradeoff: aggressive access controls can inadvertently reduce availability for legitimate users if not carefully tuned. In practice, document recovery time objectives and recovery point objectives for each service and test them. A short exercise: pick a core service and name three redundancy measures you would add to improve its availability. Availability: Designing for Resilience means plan redundancy, backups, and dos defenses early; test recovery procedures to ensure real-world availability.. In practical terms, fault tolerance, backups, and defending against dos. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Plan redundancy, backups, and DoS defenses early; test recovery procedures to ensure real-world availability.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Availability
Availability patterns
  • • Redundancy across instances and zones.
  • • Automated health checks and failover.
  • • Regular backups and verified restore procedures.
  • • Rate limiting and WAFs to reduce service overload.
Operational trap
Assuming a service is available because it passes unit tests. Availability requires full-stack testing and disaster recovery drills.
Example
A product catalog is cached across multiple regions with a primary database and read replicas. During an outage in one region, traffic reroutes to replicas and a warm standby to keep the site responsive while writes are queued and replayed.
Key Takeaway

Availability is a design goal: plan redundancy, test restores, and plan DoS defenses rather than treating them only as ops tasks.

Try this
List three mechanisms you would add to a critical microservice to reach a target 99.99% uptime.

screens.title: Threat Modeling: A Structured Process
screens.narratorSegment: Threat modeling is a repeatable process to uncover risks before they become incidents. Start by defining the system's scope: which services, data stores, and interfaces you will analyze. Next, identify assets—valuable things such as user data, payment information, and cryptographic keys. Then enumerate entry points and actors: browsers, mobile apps, third-party integrations, and privileged admins. After that, brainstorm attackers and their motivations: theft, sabotage, or fraud. Apply a systematic checklist such as STRIDE to each component to generate candidate threats. Finally, prioritize threats by likelihood and impact and propose controls that reduce risk efficiently. A concrete example: for an A P I that handles orders, the asset list might include order records and payment tokens; entry points include the public endpoint and admin console; attacker motivations include financial fraud. Prioritize threats that could expose payment tokens or enable fraudulent refunds. A common misconception is treating threat modeling as a one-time activity. Instead, make it iterative and part of design reviews, updates, and major deployments. End by asking: which asset in your next project deserves the highest protection level and why?

keyIdea.text: Scope the system, list assets and entry points, enumerate attackers, apply a checklist, then prioritize threats and controls.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Threat Modeling
Threat modeling steps
  1. Define scope and diagram the system boundaries.
  2. Identify assets and their locations.
  3. List entry points and actors.
  4. Enumerate threats using a checklist like STRIDE.
  5. Prioritize and propose mitigations.
Misconception
Threat modeling is not a single meeting; it's a living artifact updated as architecture changes.
Scenario exercise
E-commerce example: assets — user profiles and payment tokens; entry points — web checkout and admin API; attacker motivations — steal payment data or manipulate orders. Apply STRIDE to each entry point and propose countermeasures like tokenization, rate limits, and signed logs.
Key Takeaway

Threat modeling reduces surprises: define scope, list assets, check threats, and prioritize mitigations by impact.

Try
Sketch the scope for your next feature and write three assets to protect.

screens.title: STRIDE Checklist — Spotting Common Threat Types
screens.narratorSegment: STRIDE is a practical checklist to systematically generate threats for system components. Each letter maps to a threat class: Spoofing — could someone impersonate a user or service? Tampering — could data be modified? Repudiation — could an actor deny an action? Information disclosure — could data leak? Denial of Service — can attackers disrupt access? Elevation of Privilege — can an attacker gain higher rights? Use STRIDE on interfaces, data stores, and admin consoles. For example, when reviewing an A P I you might ask: can requests be replayed to spoof a user? Are inputs validated to prevent tampering such as parameter pollution? Could an attacker flood an endpoint to cause DoS? For each identified threat, record likelihood and impact and propose mitigations. A common error is stopping at identification; the useful outcome is prioritized mitigations like token rotation for spoofing, signatures for tampering, or rate limiting for DoS. Practice by taking one endpoint and writing one threat per STRIDE category and a short countermeasure for each. STRIDE Checklist — Spotting Common Threat Types means apply stride as a checklist to all components to uncover and prioritize threats with concrete mitigations.. In practical terms, spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, dos, elevation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: STRIDE Utility
keyIdea.text: Apply STRIDE as a checklist to all components to uncover and prioritize threats with concrete mitigations.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › STRIDE Checklist
STRIDE categories
  • Spoofing — impersonation; mitigation: strong authentication and token rotation.
  • Tampering — unauthorized modification; mitigation: signatures and validation.
  • Repudiation — denial of actions; mitigation: tamper-evident logs and signed receipts.
  • Information Disclosure — leaks; mitigation: encryption and access controls.
  • Denial of Service — availability attack; mitigation: rate limits and WAFs.
  • Elevation of Privilege — gaining higher rights; mitigation: least-privilege and authorization checks.
Applied example
API login endpoint: Spoofing — stolen session tokens (mitigate with secure cookie flags and rotation). Tampering — altered request data (mitigate with input validation and signing). Repudiation — user denies change (mitigate with signed receipts). Information disclosure — leaked credentials (mitigate with hashing and encryption). DoS — flood login attempts (mitigate with rate limits). Elevation — flawed role checks (mitigate with strict authorization middleware).
Key Takeaway

Use STRIDE to build a threat list and then map each item to a measurable mitigation you can test.

screens.title: Common Threat Vectors and Countermeasures
screens.narratorSegment: Threat vectors are the channels attackers use to reach your systems. Network-based attacks include port scanning and DDoS; defenses include firewalls, intrusion detection systems, and upstream scrubbing. Web vulnerabilities like S Q L injection and cross-site scripting are common in application layers; mitigations include input validation, parameterized queries, and content security policies. Social engineering, including phishing, targets people rather than systems; controls are training, multi-factor authentication, and phishing-resistant protocols. screens.title: Security Controls: Preventive, Detective, Corrective
screens.narratorSegment: Security controls fall into three practical categories. Preventive controls stop attacks before they happen—examples include encryption, access controls, and input validation. Detective controls reveal attacks in progress or after the fact—examples include intrusion detection, logging, and anomaly detection. Corrective controls restore systems and reduce damage—examples include backups, rollbacks, and incident response playbooks. When selecting controls from a threat model, choose at least one preventive and one detective control for high-impact threats, and plan corrective controls for recovery. A common design error is relying only on detective measures; detecting an attack without a plan to contain it leaves systems vulnerable. For a prioritized threat like a credential stuffing attack, prevention might be rate limiting and MFA, detection could be login anomaly detection, and corrective actions would include user notification, forced password resets, and session invalidation. Always test detective systems to ensure alerts are actionable and not noise. Ask yourself: for your top two threats, what preventive, detective, and corrective controls would you list? screens.title: Security by Design
screens.narratorSegment: Security by design means making security requirements foundational to architecture and development, not bolted on later. Practically, this begins at requirements: define sensitive assets, minimum acceptable controls, recovery objectives, and compliance needs. During architecture you select protocols, decide where to encrypt, and design control points such as authentication gateways. During implementation, enforce secure coding, peer review, and automated checks like static analysis. During testing, include threat-model-driven tests and penetration tests. Finally, in deployment and operations, manage key rotation, logging, and incident response. A vivid example: instead of adding encryption after launch, require encryption at rest and in transit from the start, plan key management, and design services that never expose raw secret material to lower-privilege components. A frequent misconception is that security by design is more costly upfront; while it requires early work, it reduces long-term remediation costs and operational surprises. Ask yourself: what two design decisions will you make differently if security is a primary requirement rather than an afterthought? screens.title: Hands-On: Basic Threat Modeling Exercise
screens.narratorSegment: Let's run a short threat-modeling exercise for an e-commerce checkout. First, list key assets: user profiles, payment information, and order records. Define entry points: browser checkout, mobile app, and admin A P I. Pick one asset and one entry point — for example, payment information via the browser checkout. Now apply STRIDE: Spoofing — session hijacking could let an attacker place orders as a user; countermeasure: secure cookies, short session lifetime, and multi-factor authentication for high-value actions. Tampering — an attacker could modify order totals or shipping addresses in transit; countermeasure: validate totals server-side and sign checkout payloads. Repudiation — users might deny purchases; countermeasure: signed receipts and tamper-evident logs. Information Disclosure — card data leakage from logs or backups; countermeasure: tokenization and encrypt backups. Denial of Service — bots could flood checkout endpoints; countermeasure: rate limits and CAPTCHA for suspicious traffic. Elevation of Privilege — an exploited client-side bug could grant admin privileges; countermeasure: strict server-side authorization checks. The practical outcome is a prioritized list with one high-impact mitigation per threat. Which mitigation would you implement first? fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this short module you will build a practical, usable picture of system security that goes beyond buzzwords. We'll anchor the work on three core goals—confidentiality, integrity, and availability—and then use a simple threat-modeling process and the STRIDE checklist to find and prioritize risks in distributed systems. You will hear concrete examples, such as encrypting data at rest and defending APIs from tampering, that show how controls map to threats. We also cover non-repudiation and accountability, and why a security-by-design approach saves time and reduces costly fixes later. By the end of this lesson you should be able to list the CIA elements, run a basic threat-modeling pass on an A P I or web flow, and recommend controls like encryption, rate limiting, and logging for common vectors. Think of this session as a toolkit: definitions to reason about risk, a repeatable checklist to find problems, and practical countermeasures you can apply when designing systems. Which part of your architecture would you inspect first for risks?

These objectives frame the skills you'll practice. First, you will learn to state and explain the CIA triad so you can reason about tradeoffs when choosing controls. Second, you'll identify common threat vectors—like injection, DDoS, and social engineering—so you can match them with countermeasures. Third, you'll perform a basic threat-modeling pass: define scope, list assets, enumerate attackers, and apply a checklist to reveal likely threats. Fourth, you'll learn to categorize and propose security controls, including preventive, detective, and corrective measures. Each objective includes a short example and a mnemonic to help you remember the task. Practically, after this lesson you should be able to run a STRIDE pass on a single A P I endpoint and recommend at least two mitigations. As you work through the activities, treat the objectives as checkpoints: can you confidently explain why a control addresses a specific threat? If not, repeat the exercise until the mapping is clear.

These additional objectives focus on two practical competencies that augment the earlier list. First, you will practice recording accountability and non-repudiation mechanisms, such as secure logs and digital signatures, so you can trace actions and resolve disputes. Second, you will learn to craft a security-by-design checklist that you can apply during requirements and architecture reviews: mandate encryption, define access control boundaries, and include backup and recovery plans. Third, you will apply STRIDE to a real A P I scenario in a hands-on exercise to see threats concretely. Fourth, you will learn to prioritize controls based on impact and likelihood rather than trying to implement every possible hardening. These skills reduce risk efficiently and make your designs practical to operate. After completing the chapter you should be able to write a short checklist to include in any architecture doc that ensures basic controls are not forgotten.

The CIA triad is a compact way to reason about what security must achieve. Confidentiality means only authorized parties can read sensitive information. A practical example is encrypting customer records at rest and encrypting service-to-service traffic to prevent eavesdropping. A common misconception is that encryption alone resolves confidentiality; keys and access controls matter too. Integrity means data remains accurate and unmodified except by authorized actions. Use hashing, digital signatures, and strict write controls to detect or prevent tampering — for example, signing configuration blobs to ensure they weren't altered before deployment. A mistake here is relying solely on network transport protection and ignoring storage integrity checks. Availability ensures authorized users can access systems when needed. Techniques include redundancy, failover, backups, and rate limiting to defend against denial-of-service. Overemphasizing confidentiality or integrity while ignoring availability can make systems unusable, so tradeoffs matter. For instance, excessively strict authentication may block legitimate traffic during peak load. When designing a service, name which of the three goals are most critical for each component, then pick controls that align with those priorities. What would you prioritize for a payment processor versus a public catalog?

Confidentiality protects data from unauthorized disclosure. In practical systems, confidentiality is implemented with layered mechanisms: encryption of data at rest, transport encryption between services, and strict access controls that limit who can read sensitive fields. A concrete example is storing customer payment details: the database should use disk or column-level encryption, communication channels should use TLS, and application roles should deny direct read access except for tokenized or masked views. Key management is frequently the weak link—if encryption keys are stored alongside data, confidentiality is broken. Rotation, limited key access, and hardware security modules are typical mitigations. Another common pitfall is assuming transport-only protection suffices; someone with database access will still read unencrypted data. Practical checks include threat-modeling who can access the database servers and ensuring backups and logs are also encrypted. Finally, consider least privilege: both human and service accounts should have the minimal read rights necessary. A short takeaway: encryption plus proper key lifecycle and access control is the correct pattern, not encryption alone. How would you protect backups and logs that contain the same sensitive fields? Confidentiality in Practice means use layered confidentiality: encrypt data, protect keys, and apply least privilege to human and service access.. In practical terms, encryption, access control, and common pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Integrity assures that data is complete, accurate, and authentic. Practically, this means detecting unauthorized changes and preventing them where possible. Common mechanisms include cryptographic hashes to detect modification, digital signatures to bind content to an identity, and tightly scoped write permissions so only authorized services can change a record. For example, sign configuration files so deployment agents can verify they are unchanged. Consider a misconfigured microservice that accepts client-supplied metadata and writes it directly to a shared database — a tampering risk. To mitigate, validate inputs, use role-based write permissions, and add end-to-end integrity checks such as message authentication codes when data moves between services. Another misconception is assuming transport-level integrity fixes storage tampering; it doesn't. Transport protections only ensure correctness in transit, not against a compromised storage subsystem. A closing question to consider: for your most critical data, would you add tamper-evident logs, signatures, or both, and why? Integrity — Detecting and Preventing Tampering means combine detection (hashes, signatures) with prevention (access controls, input validation) to protect data correctness.. In practical terms, hashes, signatures, and strict write controls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Availability ensures authorized users can reach services when they need them. Designing for availability means planning for hardware failures, software bugs, and malicious traffic. Practical strategies include redundancy across instances and zones, automated failover, regular backups with tested recovery procedures, and capacity planning. To defend against denial-of-service attacks, employ rate limiting, load shedding, and Web Application Firewalls; for large-scale attacks, use network-level protections and upstream scrubbing services. A common mistake is treating availability as purely an operational concern; architects must design systems with availability goals in mind, for example by selecting stateless services where possible and separating critical services into independent failure domains. Another tradeoff: aggressive access controls can inadvertently reduce availability for legitimate users if not carefully tuned. In practice, document recovery time objectives and recovery point objectives for each service and test them. A short exercise: pick a core service and name three redundancy measures you would add to improve its availability. Availability: Designing for Resilience means plan redundancy, backups, and dos defenses early; test recovery procedures to ensure real-world availability.. In practical terms, fault tolerance, backups, and defending against dos. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Threat modeling is a repeatable process to uncover risks before they become incidents. Start by defining the system's scope: which services, data stores, and interfaces you will analyze. Next, identify assets—valuable things such as user data, payment information, and cryptographic keys. Then enumerate entry points and actors: browsers, mobile apps, third-party integrations, and privileged admins. After that, brainstorm attackers and their motivations: theft, sabotage, or fraud. Apply a systematic checklist such as STRIDE to each component to generate candidate threats. Finally, prioritize threats by likelihood and impact and propose controls that reduce risk efficiently. A concrete example: for an A P I that handles orders, the asset list might include order records and payment tokens; entry points include the public endpoint and admin console; attacker motivations include financial fraud. Prioritize threats that could expose payment tokens or enable fraudulent refunds. A common misconception is treating threat modeling as a one-time activity. Instead, make it iterative and part of design reviews, updates, and major deployments. End by asking: which asset in your next project deserves the highest protection level and why?

STRIDE is a practical checklist to systematically generate threats for system components. Each letter maps to a threat class: Spoofing — could someone impersonate a user or service? Tampering — could data be modified? Repudiation — could an actor deny an action? Information disclosure — could data leak? Denial of Service — can attackers disrupt access? Elevation of Privilege — can an attacker gain higher rights? Use STRIDE on interfaces, data stores, and admin consoles. For example, when reviewing an A P I you might ask: can requests be replayed to spoof a user? Are inputs validated to prevent tampering such as parameter pollution? Could an attacker flood an endpoint to cause DoS? For each identified threat, record likelihood and impact and propose mitigations. A common error is stopping at identification; the useful outcome is prioritized mitigations like token rotation for spoofing, signatures for tampering, or rate limiting for DoS. Practice by taking one endpoint and writing one threat per STRIDE category and a short countermeasure for each. Network-based attacks include port scanning and DDoS; defenses include firewalls, intrusion detection systems, and upstream scrubbing. Web vulnerabilities like S Q L injection and cross-site scripting are common in application layers; mitigations include input validation, parameterized queries, and content security policies. Social engineering, including phishing, targets people rather than systems; controls are training, multi-factor authentication, and phishing-resistant protocols. Insider threats come from privileged users who misuse access; use strict role separation, monitoring, and just-in-time privileges. A practical example: protecting a web form requires sanitizing inputs to prevent injection, rate limiting to reduce automated attacks, and monitoring to detect suspicious patterns. Common Threat Vectors and Countermeasures means match vectors to layered defenses: preventive controls stop attacks, detective controls find them, and corrective controls restore systems.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Security controls fall into three practical categories. Preventive controls stop attacks before they happen—examples include encryption, access controls, and input validation. Detective controls reveal attacks in progress or after the fact—examples include intrusion detection, logging, and anomaly detection. Corrective controls restore systems and reduce damage—examples include backups, rollbacks, and incident response playbooks. When selecting controls from a threat model, choose at least one preventive and one detective control for high-impact threats, and plan corrective controls for recovery. A common design error is relying only on detective measures; detecting an attack without a plan to contain it leaves systems vulnerable. For a prioritized threat like a credential stuffing attack, prevention might be rate limiting and MFA, detection could be login anomaly detection, and corrective actions would include user notification, forced password resets, and session invalidation. Always test detective systems to ensure alerts are actionable and not noise. Ask yourself: for your top two threats, what preventive, detective, and corrective controls would you list? Security by design means making security requirements foundational to architecture and development, not bolted on later. Practically, this begins at requirements: define sensitive assets, minimum acceptable controls, recovery objectives, and compliance needs. During architecture you select protocols, decide where to encrypt, and design control points such as authentication gateways. During implementation, enforce secure coding, peer review, and automated checks like static analysis. During testing, include threat-model-driven tests and penetration tests. Finally, in deployment and operations, manage key rotation, logging, and incident response. A vivid example: instead of adding encryption after launch, require encryption at rest and in transit from the start, plan key management, and design services that never expose raw secret material to lower-privilege components. A frequent misconception is that security by design is more costly upfront; while it requires early work, it reduces long-term remediation costs and operational surprises. Ask yourself: what two design decisions will you make differently if security is a primary requirement rather than an afterthought? Security by Design means make security requirements part of every lifecycle stage: requirements, architecture, implementation, testing, and operations.. Let's run a short threat-modeling exercise for an e-commerce checkout. First, list key assets: user profiles, payment information, and order records. Define entry points: browser checkout, mobile app, and admin A P I. Pick one asset and one entry point — for example, payment information via the browser checkout. Now apply STRIDE: Spoofing — session hijacking could let an attacker place orders as a user; countermeasure: secure cookies, short session lifetime, and multi-factor authentication for high-value actions. Tampering — an attacker could modify order totals or shipping addresses in transit; countermeasure: validate totals server-side and sign checkout payloads. Repudiation — users might deny purchases; countermeasure: signed receipts and tamper-evident logs. Information Disclosure — card data leakage from logs or backups; countermeasure: tokenization and encrypt backups. Denial of Service — bots could flood checkout endpoints; countermeasure: rate limits and CAPTCHA for suspicious traffic. Elevation of Privilege — an exploited client-side bug could grant admin privileges; countermeasure: strict server-side authorization checks. The practical outcome is a prioritized list with one high-impact mitigation per threat. Which mitigation would you implement first? Let's summarize the essentials you should carry forward. First, the CIA triad—confidentiality, integrity, and availability—are the primary goals for designing secure systems. Second, STRIDE is a practical checklist to uncover threats across Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, and Elevation of Privilege. Third, threat modeling turns diagrams and asset lists into prioritized mitigations you can implement. Keep these three concepts as tools: goals to measure against, a checklist to generate threats, and a process to prioritize controls. When in doubt, ask which CIA goal a component must meet, run STRIDE on each entry point, and pick layered defensive controls that include preventive and detective measures. This practice will help you design systems that are both secure and operationally practical. Which of these concepts will you apply first in your next architecture review?
